items.prompt: A web tier has balanced CPU, memory, network, and EBS demand with no dominant bottleneck. Which EC2 starting point is appropriate?
constraints: The application is general purpose.
Utilization is measured.
No accelerator or local-disk requirement exists.

options.text: Evaluate a current general-purpose EC2 family and size it from measured CPU, memory, network, EBS, latency, and scaling requirements.
Choose the largest memory-optimized instance because more memory always improves every web tier.
Choose an accelerated instance because all web applications benefit from GPUs.
Choose instance store only because general-purpose instances cannot use EBS.

feedback.Reason: Balanced workloads should start with a general-purpose family and be sized from the complete resource profile.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 families expose different ratios of CPU, memory, network, storage, and accelerators.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks representative traffic and selects the smallest family and size that meets the SLO with scaling headroom.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory-optimized can waste CPU, GPUs are not universal web requirements, and general-purpose instances use EBS where supported.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A general-purpose family is a starting hypothesis and must be revisited when the dominant resource changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An oversized memory ratio can increase cost without fixing the bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Accelerators add cost and require application support.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EBS is a normal storage option for EC2 instances.

items.prompt: A service is CPU-bound after profiling and has modest memory demand. Which EC2 family should be compared?
constraints: CPU is the measured bottleneck.
Memory usage is stable.
The application scales horizontally.

options.text: Compare a compute-optimized EC2 family and size it from sustained CPU, network, EBS, licensing, and scaling measurements.
Choose a memory-optimized family solely because it has more vCPUs in one size.
Add EBS IOPS to solve a pure CPU saturation problem.
Use GPU instances without a parallel accelerator workload.

feedback.Reason: Compute-optimized families are candidates for sustained CPU-intensive workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 family ratios and processor characteristics differ; the correct family follows the dominant measured resource.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates CPU generation, network and EBS limits, licensing, and horizontal scaling before changing family.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory capacity does not solve CPU saturation, EBS does not add compute, and an unused GPU wastes cost.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher CPU density can expose a different network, memory, or license bottleneck.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Memory-optimized ratios do not directly address a CPU-bound workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Storage performance cannot remove CPU execution saturation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Accelerators require software support and suitable parallel work.

items.prompt: An in-memory analytics service frequently pages because its dataset exceeds available RAM, while CPU remains moderate. What should be evaluated?
constraints: Memory is the measured bottleneck.
The working set is larger than current RAM.
The application benefits from scale-up or sharding.

options.text: Evaluate a memory-optimized family, comparing RAM, network, EBS, NUMA behavior, cost, and the application's scale-out alternative.
Choose compute-optimized instances because paging is a CPU problem.
Increase EBS IOPS and leave insufficient RAM unchanged.
Use a GPU because memory pressure automatically benefits from graphics memory.

feedback.Reason: Memory-optimized instances are candidates when RAM, not CPU, limits the working set.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 memory-optimized families provide higher memory ratios and may expose different network or NUMA characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models working-set growth, instance memory, network, EBS, and whether partitioning or a managed data service is better.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU density does not fix paging, EBS cannot substitute for RAM, and GPU memory is not general system memory.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scale-up can reduce paging but increase failure blast radius and cost; scale-out may require application changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Compute density does not add the required system memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Storage latency is not equivalent to RAM latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: GPU memory is specialized and does not replace host memory automatically.

items.prompt: A distributed database needs very high local NVMe throughput and can replicate data across nodes. Which EC2 family characteristic is relevant?
constraints: The application uses local ephemeral storage.
Data is replicated independently.
Local I/O is the measured bottleneck.

options.text: Evaluate a storage-optimized family with local NVMe, while designing data replication, replacement, rebuild, and loss behavior explicitly.
Use instance store as the sole durable copy because NVMe is persistent across termination.
Choose memory-optimized instances and ignore local storage throughput.
Use S3 as a transparent local block device for the database.

feedback.Reason: Storage-optimized families can fit local NVMe workloads when the application owns durability and rebuild.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Local instance store provides high local performance but is ephemeral and tied to the instance lifecycle.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates NVMe count and bandwidth, replication factor, failure replacement, and recovery time before selection.
Details.errorCorrection: Instance store is not durable alone, memory ratio does not solve local I/O, and S3 is object storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local NVMe improves performance but increases replacement and data-loss complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Instance store data can be lost when the instance stops or terminates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Memory-optimized capacity does not provide the required local storage path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object storage is not a block-device replacement without an application layer.

items.prompt: A low-average-CPU service has short bursts and can tolerate CPU throttling after prolonged sustained use. Which option should be compared?
constraints: Average CPU is low.
Bursts are intermittent.
Credit behavior is acceptable and monitored.

options.text: Evaluate a burstable EC2 instance and model baseline performance, credit accumulation and depletion, burst duration, and application SLOs.
Use a burstable instance for a permanently CPU-saturated workload without a credit model.
Assume burst credits increase network bandwidth without limits.
Disable CPU monitoring because bursts are expected.

feedback.Reason: Burstable instances fit variable CPU demand only when baseline and credit behavior meet the workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: T instances provide a baseline and can use CPU credits for bursts, with documented behavior and monitoring.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures credit balance and CPU, alarms before depletion, and moves sustained workloads to a fixed-performance family.
Details.errorCorrection: Sustained saturation depletes credits, credits do not control network bandwidth, and monitoring is required.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Burstable pricing can be efficient for intermittent demand but creates a performance dependency on credit state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Permanent saturation is not a safe burstable workload assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CPU credits do not provide unlimited network capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Credit and CPU metrics are needed to detect the boundary.

items.prompt: A Linux service is portable across architectures and the team wants better price-performance. Which EC2 selection path is valid?
constraints: The runtime and dependencies support Arm.
The image and native libraries are available.
Performance is benchmarked on representative traffic.

options.text: Evaluate a Graviton-based instance family, rebuild or select compatible images and libraries, and benchmark performance and operational compatibility before migration.
Move to Arm without checking native binaries because Linux applications are always architecture-neutral.
Use a GPU because architecture changes require graphics acceleration.
Run x86-only binaries unchanged on Arm and ignore runtime errors.

feedback.Reason: Graviton can improve price-performance when the software supply chain and workload are compatible.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Arm-based EC2 requires compatible AMIs, binaries, libraries, containers, and operational tooling.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner builds a canary, validates dependencies and performance, and keeps a rollback path during the architecture transition.
Details.errorCorrection: Native binaries are not universally portable, GPUs are unrelated, and ignoring runtime failures is not a migration plan.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Architecture migration can reduce cost but adds build, test, and vendor-compatibility work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Native dependencies can be architecture-specific.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A CPU architecture migration does not imply a GPU requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Incompatible binaries can fail to start or behave incorrectly.

items.prompt: A machine-learning inference service requires CUDA-compatible GPU kernels and measured parallel tensor workload. Which instance type should be evaluated?
constraints: The framework supports the accelerator.
GPU utilization is measurable.
Latency and throughput targets are explicit.

options.text: Evaluate a GPU-accelerated EC2 family with compatible drivers and framework, sizing GPU memory, host CPU, network, EBS, and utilization together.
Use a general-purpose instance because GPU memory is never relevant to inference.
Use an Inferentia instance without checking framework compilation or model support.
Use a larger EBS volume as a substitute for GPU parallelism.

feedback.Reason: A CUDA-oriented workload can justify GPUs when the software and model support them.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Accelerated EC2 families differ in accelerator type, memory, host resources, and framework support.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect benchmarks batch size, GPU memory, host bottlenecks, network, and cost per inference.
Details.errorCorrection: General-purpose CPU does not provide GPU parallelism, Inferentia needs a different software path, and EBS cannot replace compute.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: GPU capacity can be expensive when utilization is low or model support is incomplete.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GPU memory and parallel kernels are central to the stated workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Inferentia requires compatible compilation and framework support.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage capacity does not perform tensor computation.

items.prompt: An inference workload can compile to AWS Neuron and prioritizes cost per inference over CUDA compatibility. Which option should be compared?
constraints: The model and framework support Neuron.
Inference throughput is measurable.
The team can operate the compiled artifact.

options.text: Evaluate Inferentia-based EC2 instances with Neuron-compatible compilation, model latency, accelerator utilization, host resources, and cost per request.
Choose GPU instances automatically because every ML model requires CUDA.
Choose memory-optimized instances and ignore accelerator support.
Use CPU instances without benchmarking the supported accelerator path.

feedback.Reason: Inferentia is a candidate for supported inference workloads when its software path and economics fit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS Neuron provides the compilation and runtime path for supported Inferentia workloads.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests model operators, compilation, batch size, latency, utilization, and fallback behavior before committing.
Details.errorCorrection: GPU and Inferentia have different software and economics, memory-only instances do not accelerate inference, and unbenchmarked CPU is an assumption.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Specialized accelerators can lower unit cost but reduce model portability and require a compatible toolchain.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CUDA is not required when the model supports the Neuron path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Host memory alone does not provide inference acceleration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CPU may work but cannot be selected without measuring the target economics and latency.

items.prompt: A distributed training workload uses a supported framework and needs large-scale tensor compute. Which EC2 decision is relevant?
constraints: The training stack supports the accelerator.
The job can be distributed.
Interconnect and storage throughput are measured.

options.text: Evaluate Trainium-based instances with supported framework tooling, accelerator memory, interconnect, data pipeline, checkpointing, and utilization measured together.
Choose a CPU-only family because training performance depends only on dataset size.
Use GPU instances without checking whether the training framework supports the selected accelerator.
Use S3 request rate as a substitute for accelerator throughput.

feedback.Reason: Trainium can fit supported distributed training workloads, but compute, interconnect, input, and checkpoint paths must be measured.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Accelerated training instances expose specialized chips, memory, networking, and software requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect benchmarks scaling efficiency, data loading, checkpointing, failure recovery, and cost per training step.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU-only selection ignores tensor compute, GPU and Trainium have different support paths, and S3 request rate is not compute throughput.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Specialized training hardware can improve economics but narrows framework and operator compatibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Dataset size does not determine the best compute engine by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Accelerator support must be verified for the exact framework and model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object request rate does not measure tensor execution or interconnect performance.

items.prompt: A team chooses an EC2 size by vCPU count alone, but the application is memory-bound and network-heavy. What should change?
constraints: Memory and network are measured bottlenecks.
The family is not yet fixed.
The workload has an SLO.

options.text: Compare the family ratio and size across memory, network, EBS, CPU, and application metrics rather than selecting from vCPU count alone.
Choose the fewest vCPUs because fewer cores always improve memory performance.
Choose the most vCPUs regardless of memory and network limits.
Increase EBS capacity to increase instance network bandwidth.

feedback.Reason: EC2 size selection is multidimensional and vCPU count alone can hide the actual bottleneck.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Each instance size exposes a resource profile and documented network or EBS limits alongside vCPUs and memory.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses load tests and CloudWatch or application metrics to choose the smallest SLO-compliant size.
Details.errorCorrection: Fewer or more vCPUs do not automatically fix memory or network, and capacity does not change instance bandwidth.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A balanced size may cost more than a CPU-only choice but reduce saturation and waste.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Reducing CPU does not guarantee more memory or network capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Extra CPU can be idle while memory or network remains saturated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EBS volume capacity is not instance network bandwidth.

items.prompt: A compute instance has low CPU utilization but misses an inter-service throughput target. Which EC2 sizing signal is most relevant?
constraints: Network throughput is the measured bottleneck.
The application uses a finite instance path.
Horizontal scaling is possible.

options.text: Compare instance network bandwidth, packet rate, placement, ENI limits, and application connection behavior rather than increasing CPU blindly.
Choose a larger memory size because network performance is always proportional to RAM.
Increase EBS IOPS because EBS settings control all network traffic.
Move the instance to another Region to increase local network bandwidth.

feedback.Reason: EC2 network performance has instance and topology boundaries independent of CPU utilization.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance type, ENI or packet limits, placement, and application connection patterns can cap network throughput.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures bytes and packets, checks instance documentation and network topology, and chooses scale-up or scale-out from evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: RAM is not a universal network control, EBS is a separate path, and a Region move adds latency rather than solving the local limit.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Larger or distributed instances can improve bandwidth but may add cost, cross-AZ traffic, or coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Memory size does not universally determine network bandwidth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EBS throughput is not application network throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A Region move usually increases latency and changes failure domains.

items.prompt: An EC2 instance has a high-performance EBS volume but the application cannot reach its provisioned throughput. What should be checked?
constraints: EBS is the measured path.
The instance type has a documented EBS limit.
The volume setting is appropriate.

options.text: Check whether the instance is EBS-optimized and whether its EBS bandwidth and IOPS limits support the volume configuration and workload.
Increase the volume capacity without checking instance EBS bandwidth.
Move the volume to S3 to increase block throughput.
Add CPU cores because EBS bandwidth is unlimited on every instance.

feedback.Reason: The EC2 EBS path can be the bottleneck even when the volume is provisioned correctly.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance types expose EBS bandwidth and operation limits; EBS optimization provides dedicated or appropriate storage performance characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner correlates volume and instance metrics and chooses a compatible instance or volume configuration.
Details.errorCorrection: Capacity is not bandwidth, S3 is not block storage, and CPU count does not make the EBS path unlimited.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A larger instance can improve EBS performance but raises compute cost and may expose another bottleneck.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Volume capacity does not automatically remove the instance path limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 cannot replace an attached block volume without an application change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CPU resources do not imply unlimited EBS bandwidth.

items.prompt: A licensing or hardware application requires direct access to physical resources and cannot run with a hypervisor abstraction. Which option should be evaluated?
constraints: The vendor confirms a bare-metal requirement.
The application is otherwise EC2-compatible.
Operational and recovery needs are known.

options.text: Evaluate a supported bare-metal EC2 instance, confirming the exact licensing, device, network, storage, boot, and replacement behavior.
Use a virtualized instance because all hardware-sensitive software is equivalent under a hypervisor.
Use Lambda because serverless functions expose physical hardware directly.
Use instance store as a substitute for bare-metal execution.

feedback.Reason: Bare-metal instances are a candidate when a verified workload or licensing requirement needs them.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 offers bare-metal and virtualized options with different device and virtualization characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect confirms vendor support, AMI and driver behavior, network and storage access, and replacement planning.
Details.errorCorrection: Virtualization may violate a vendor requirement, Lambda has a different execution model, and instance store is only storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Bare metal can constrain capacity and fleet flexibility and should not be selected without a concrete requirement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A stated bare-metal requirement cannot be dismissed without vendor evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda does not expose a customer-controlled bare-metal environment.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage choice does not change the compute virtualization model.

items.prompt: A commercial database requires terabytes of RAM on one host and cannot be sharded yet. Which EC2 category should be compared?
constraints: The database is scale-up constrained.
RAM is the dominant resource.
Licensing and failure recovery are explicit.

options.text: Evaluate high-memory EC2 options, comparing RAM, CPU, NUMA, network, EBS, licensing, single-host blast radius, and recovery.
Use a small general-purpose instance and rely on swap for database memory.
Use a GPU because GPU memory is identical to database host memory.
Use Lambda because a database can always be split into functions.

feedback.Reason: High-memory EC2 options fit scale-up databases whose working set cannot yet be partitioned.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: High-memory instances provide very large host memory and have specific CPU, network, EBS, licensing, and recovery characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner verifies vendor certification, database memory use, EBS path, restart time, and the impact of losing one large host.
Details.errorCorrection: Swap is not equivalent to RAM, GPU memory is specialized, and Lambda is not a database host.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scale-up simplifies an unsharded database but concentrates failure and can increase licensing and recovery cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Swap latency and capacity do not satisfy a large in-memory database requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GPU memory does not replace host RAM for a database.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lambda execution units do not provide a persistent database host.

items.prompt: A network appliance requires very high packet rate and bandwidth, while CPU and memory are moderate. Which EC2 family characteristic matters?
constraints: Packet processing is measured.
The appliance is supported on EC2.
The VPC topology and ENI limits are known.

options.text: Evaluate network-optimized or high-network-bandwidth instances and validate packet rate, ENI limits, placement, CPU, memory, and acceleration support.
Choose memory-optimized instances because packets are stored in RAM.
Choose the cheapest instance and assume VPC networking is uniform across sizes.
Increase EBS volume size to increase packets per second.

feedback.Reason: Network-intensive appliances need an instance and topology with suitable bandwidth and packet or ENI limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance types differ in network bandwidth, packet processing, ENI counts, and supported networking features.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures pps and bytes, validates placement and security paths, and chooses a size with headroom.
Details.errorCorrection: RAM and EBS capacity do not provide network packet capacity, and EC2 networking is not uniform across sizes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: High-network instances can cost more and still require correct VPC design and appliance licensing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Memory is not the primary network capacity control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance network limits vary materially by size and family.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EBS volume capacity does not increase network packets per second.

items.prompt: A team compares an older and newer EC2 generation using only vCPU count. What evidence is missing?
constraints: The application has a measurable SLO.
Processor generations differ.
The workload uses CPU, memory, network, and storage.

options.text: Benchmark the exact workload across processor, memory, network, EBS, licensing, startup, and scaling dimensions and compare cost per useful unit of work.
Assume equal vCPU counts provide equal performance and price efficiency.
Choose the newer generation without checking AMI or driver compatibility.
Choose the older generation because it has known behavior regardless of cost or capacity.

feedback.Reason: Instance generation changes more than vCPU count and must be tested against the workload and compatibility contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Processor architecture, memory, network, EBS, virtualization, and pricing can differ by generation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner runs a representative canary and evaluates throughput, latency, utilization, failure behavior, and unit economics.
Details.errorCorrection: Equal vCPU counts are not equal performance, newer hardware can expose compatibility gaps, and older hardware can cost more or lack capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: New generations often improve economics but require an explicit compatibility and rollback check.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: vCPU count is not a complete performance equivalence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AMI, drivers, architecture, and licensing need validation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Familiarity does not prove current cost, capacity, or SLO fit.

items.prompt: A licensed database is limited by the number of physical cores or vCPUs it can use. Which EC2 selection detail needs review?
constraints: The license has a documented metric.
The instance supports the required configuration.
Database performance must remain adequate.

options.text: Compare instance CPU options, visible vCPUs, physical-core licensing, database parallelism, price, and measured throughput before selecting a size.
Choose the largest instance because licensed software always scales linearly.
Ignore license rules because vCPU count is only a billing label.
Use a GPU to avoid all CPU licensing constraints without vendor support.

feedback.Reason: EC2 CPU configuration and licensing are linked and must be evaluated with database performance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Some EC2 options allow CPU configuration while instance size, physical cores, vCPUs, and licensing vary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates vendor terms and tests the database at the selected CPU topology rather than maximizing unused capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Software does not always scale linearly, license rules are real constraints, and GPUs do not remove CPU licensing without support.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Reducing licensed cores can cut cost but may reduce throughput and increase per-unit work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More instance capacity can increase license cost without proportional throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: License metrics are contractual, not optional labels.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A GPU does not replace a database CPU license by assumption.

items.prompt: A development fleet should pause for hours and resume with memory state, while production workloads need rapid replacement. Which EC2 sizing review is relevant?
constraints: The environment is non-production.
Memory state can be preserved.
Application and AMI support hibernation.

options.text: Evaluate hibernation support, instance family and size limits, encrypted root storage, memory cost, resume time, and whether stopping is safer than preserving state.
Assume every EC2 instance can hibernate with any root volume and memory size.
Use instance store as the hibernation image because it is always persistent.
Hibernate a production fleet without testing resume, credentials, and state validity.

feedback.Reason: Hibernation is an instance and workload capability with storage, encryption, memory, and resume constraints.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 hibernation saves memory state to the root EBS volume and is limited by instance, AMI, and workload support.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates support and resume behavior in the target size, protects the root volume, and uses it only where preserved state is useful.
Details.errorCorrection: Support is not universal, instance store is ephemeral, and untested production resume can restore stale or invalid state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Hibernation can reduce startup cost or time but stores memory and complicates state management.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Hibernation has documented support and configuration limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance store is not a durable hibernation target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Production state must be validated before relying on resume.

items.prompt: A cache-heavy application needs very low-latency scratch space and can rebuild all data from a durable source. Which instance feature should be evaluated?
constraints: The data is disposable or reproducible.
Local latency is the bottleneck.
The application can detect and refill a lost cache.

options.text: Evaluate an instance type with local NVMe instance store, while designing cache warm-up, loss detection, replacement, and durable-source access.
Use local NVMe as the only database source of truth.
Use an EBS snapshot as a synchronous local cache.
Use S3 directly for every sub-millisecond cache read without a local layer.

feedback.Reason: Ephemeral local NVMe can fit rebuildable scratch or cache workloads when loss behavior is explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance store offers local performance but data is tied to the instance and is not a durable independent copy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps a durable source, detects instance replacement, warms the cache gradually, and protects startup from thundering herds.
Details.errorCorrection: A source of truth on instance store is unsafe, snapshots are not synchronous cache, and remote S3 latency is not sub-millisecond by default.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local performance improves latency but requires application-aware recovery and fleet placement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Instance store can be lost and is not a durable source of truth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Snapshots are point-in-time copies, not synchronous cache memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object storage needs a local or application cache for such latency.

items.prompt: Two EC2 families both meet a latency target, but one uses more capacity and has lower unit price. What comparison is correct?
constraints: Both options are functionally compatible.
Utilization and scaling are measured.
Availability and licensing costs matter.

options.text: Compare cost per useful request or job including instance price, utilization, scaling count, storage and transfer, licensing, failure capacity, and operational effort.
Choose the lowest hourly price regardless of required instance count and utilization.
Choose the highest benchmark score without checking application workload or availability.
Use one family for all services to avoid measuring different ratios.

feedback.Reason: Family economics are workload and fleet decisions, not a single hourly price or benchmark score.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance family price, performance, utilization, scaling, licensing, storage, network, and failure headroom interact.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect runs representative tests and compares steady state, peaks, replacement, and cost per useful unit.
Details.errorCorrection: A cheap instance can require more nodes, a benchmark can misrepresent the workload, and uniformity can force waste.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Standardizing a compatible family can reduce operations but should not override a material cost or performance mismatch.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Hourly price ignores fleet size and useful throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Synthetic peak scores do not prove application fit or resilience.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Different workloads can need different family ratios.

items.prompt: A production instance runs at 90 percent CPU during normal peaks and has no spare network or EBS headroom. What is the design concern?
constraints: The peak is recurring.
The service must survive a node replacement.
Scaling takes time.

options.text: Add measured capacity headroom or scale-out capacity, check network and EBS limits separately, and test replacement and peak behavior against the SLO.
Keep the size because high utilization proves the instance is cost-efficient.
Increase only the EBS volume size to create compute and network headroom.
Disable health checks so replacement does not interrupt the overloaded node.

feedback.Reason: Near-saturation leaves little response margin for peaks, failures, and scaling delay.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 CPU, network, EBS, and replacement capacity are separate constraints that can be saturated at different times.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets thresholds, adds capacity before the boundary, and validates failure and scale-out response.
Details.errorCorrection: High utilization can increase latency and failure risk, volume size does not add compute, and disabling health checks hides failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom costs money but is part of the availability and latency design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cost efficiency is not achieved if SLOs fail during normal peaks or replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Volume capacity does not add CPU, network, or instance EBS bandwidth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks are needed to remove failed or unhealthy capacity.

items.prompt: A design review selects EC2 instances from a generic benchmark but has not identified the application's limiting resource. What decision is missing?
constraints: The workload has measurable resource signals.
The application has an availability target.
The fleet can scale or change family.

options.text: Profile CPU, memory, network, EBS or local storage, accelerator, licensing, scaling, failure, and cost signals, then choose the family and size that meet the complete SLO.
Choose the instance with the largest vCPU count because more compute always dominates.
Choose the most expensive family to guarantee performance.
Choose one family permanently and skip workload measurement.

feedback.Reason: EC2 selection is a constrained workload decision and needs the actual limiting resource and full path evidence.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Families and sizes trade CPU, memory, storage, network, accelerators, availability, and cost.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures representative and peak behavior, selects a canonical family, and keeps a testable scale or replacement path.
Details.errorCorrection: vCPU count can leave another resource saturated, expensive hardware is not guaranteed fit, and permanent assumptions become stale.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A broader profile takes test effort but prevents overprovisioning and hidden instance limits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU is only one resource and may not be the bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Price does not guarantee workload compatibility or availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Without measurement, family choice is an unsupported assumption.
